4. TRACK CLEARANCE REQUIREMENTS

4.1 The Authority's directive mandates minimum track clearance of 600 mm. Record status: current. This clearance applies to all personnel, tools, and equipment when working on or near the track.

4.2 The 600 mm clearance is measured from the nearest running rail face to the closest point of the person, tool, or equipment. This distance is the minimum separation required at all times, including during work activities, rest periods, and when moving along the track.

4.3 The clearance requirement applies to:
- Personnel walking along or across the track
- Hand tools, including hammers, bars, and measuring equipment
- Plant and machinery, including trolleys, grinders, and tampers

- Trains are travelling at high speed
- The track is curved and sight distance is limited
- Weather conditions reduce visibility
- The worksite is in a tunnel or cutting
- Plant or equipment is being operated

4.6 Do not place tools or materials closer than 600 mm to the running rail, even temporarily. If you need to put something down while working, place it on the opposite side of the track or at a safe distance.

4.7 Check that your worksite layout maintains the clearance before work commences and after any change in activities. The person in charge of the worksite is responsible for ensuring compliance.

SAFETY BRIEFING 2024-11
ISSUED: 4 November 2024
EFFECTIVE: Immediately
ISSUING OFFICE: PCRMD Safety Office
DISTRIBUTION: All staff, contractors, and visitors

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 This briefing supplements the PCRMD Safety Management System and the Track Work Safety Manual. It applies to all rail maintenance activities, including planned works, fault response, inspections, and possessions.

1.2 This briefing remains in effect until superseded. A record of this briefing is held in the safety office. Safety Briefing 2024-11 issued date 2024-11-04 date. Record status: historical.

1.3 All supervisors must confirm that their teams have read and understood this briefing before commencing work. Confirmation is to be recorded on the team briefing sheet and returned to the safety office by close of business Friday 8 November 2024.

2. HAZARD ALERTS – RECENT INCIDENTS

2.1 Incident: Near miss with track vehicle at the Westport yard crossover, 28 October 2024.

A track vehicle moved through the crossover while a small team was walking back to the compound after completing a ballast inspection. The lookout was in position but was focused on the main line rather than the yard lead. The vehicle operator sounded the horn and the team cleared the track with approximately 20 seconds to spare.

Contributing factors:
- Lookout positioned on the wrong side of the group
- Yard movements not included in the pre-work risk assessment
- Team walked along the track instead of the designated walkway

Actions required:
- Yard and depot movements must be included in the pre-work brief even when the work is on the main line
- Lookouts must position themselves to cover all possible approach directions
- Use the designated walkway whenever it is available, even if it adds time

2.2 Incident: Hand injury during rail grinding, 30 October 2024.

A crew member sustained a crush injury to the left hand while adjusting a grinding stone. The machine was not isolated and the crew member placed their hand between the stone and the guard while the wheel was still spinning down.

Contributing factors:
- Machine not isolated before adjustment
- Crew member attempting a quick adjustment rather than stopping the machine
- Inadequate supervision of the task

Actions required:
- All adjustments to grinding equipment must be carried out with the machine isolated and the wheel at a complete stop
- No adjustment is permitted while the wheel is spinning, regardless of how long the machine takes to stop
- Supervisors must check that isolation is in place before any adjustment begins

2.3 Incident: Spotting of a broken rail near the 87.4 km mark, 1 November 2024.

A track patrol identified a broken rail on the down line. The rail had a transverse break at the web. The patrol reported it immediately and the line was blocked. No train passed over the break.

Actions required:
- Continue to report any suspected rail defect immediately, even if you are not certain
- Do not attempt to assess the severity of a defect while trains are running
- Ensure your patrol route includes checking the full rail section, not just the head

2.4 Hazard alert: Increased kangaroo activity on the corridor between the 92 km and 98 km marks.

Recent reports indicate a higher than usual number of kangaroos moving across the track in this section, particularly around dawn and dusk. While this is not a direct track worker hazard, it can cause distractions and sudden movements by drivers of track vehicles.

Actions required:
- Reduce speed when driving track vehicles through this section at dawn and dusk
- Be alert for animals moving onto the track ahead of you
- Report any collisions or near misses with animals to your supervisor

2.5 Hazard alert: Dusty ballast conditions in the cuttings near the 74 km mark.

The recent dry weather has left ballast dusty in the cuttings. This reduces visibility when working near the track and can make footing unstable on slopes.

Actions required:
- Use additional caution when walking or working on ballast in these areas
- Wear dust masks if dust is affecting your breathing
- Water down the area if dust becomes excessive and this is practical
Safety Briefing 2024-11
Briefing No. 2024-11-04
Issue Date: 4 November 2024
Effective: Immediately

This briefing is issued to all track maintenance, patrol, and track vehicle staff. It follows the incident and hazard alerts in the earlier sections of this briefing (Sections 2.1 to 2.5). Please read this entire document carefully, sign the acknowledgement sheet at the end, and return it to your supervisor by 8 November 2024.

Section 3 – General Safety Reminders

The following reminders apply to all work activities on the corridor, regardless of the specific task. They are not new rules, but they are frequently overlooked. Please treat them as mandatory.

3.1 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

- Hard hat, hi-vis vest, and safety boots are to be worn at all times when on or near the track. This includes walking to and from the work site, and during breaks if you are still within the track corridor.
- Safety glasses should be worn when grinding, cutting, or doing any task that may produce flying particles. If you wear prescription glasses, you must wear approved over-glasses.
- Hearing protection must be worn when operating or working near powered equipment, including grinders, tampers, and generators. If you have to raise your voice to be heard by someone an arm's length away, you need hearing protection.
- Gloves are required for handling rail, sleepers, ballast, or any material with sharp edges. Do not wear gloves when operating rotating machinery such as grinders or drills – they can get caught.
- Dust masks are to be worn where dust is present, including the dusty ballast conditions mentioned in Section 2.5. If you are unsure whether a mask is needed, ask your supervisor.

3.2 Track Access and Lookout

- Never enter the track corridor without a valid track access permit and a current briefing on the day's protection arrangements.
- If you are working under a lookout, you must maintain voice or radio contact with the lookout at all times. If you lose contact, stop work and move to a safe location.
- The lookout's instructions are to be followed immediately, without question. Do not stop to gather tools or equipment – your safety is more important than any tool.
- When walking along the track, always face oncoming traffic unless you are specifically instructed otherwise. Stay clear of the gauge corner of the rail where possible.
- Do not cross the track at unprotected locations. Use the designated crossing points.

3.3 Track Vehicle Operation

- All track vehicles must be operated by a person holding the appropriate competency for that vehicle type.
- Conduct a pre-start inspection of the vehicle each day before use. Check brakes, lights, horns, and any attachments.
- Do not carry passengers unless the vehicle is fitted with approved seating and seatbelts for the number of passengers.
- When driving through the corridor, particularly in the sections with increased kangaroo activity (92 km to 98 km), reduce speed and be prepared to stop suddenly.
- Never leave a track vehicle unattended on the line unless it has been properly secured and the area protected.

3.4 Manual Handling and Lifting

- Assess the load before lifting. If it is too heavy or awkward, use a mechanical aid or get help.
- Use proper lifting technique: bend at the knees, keep your back straight, and hold the load close to your body.
- Do not twist your body while carrying a load. Turn your feet first.
- Report any manual handling injuries, no matter how minor, to your supervisor.

Section 4 – Frequently Asked Questions

The following questions have been raised by staff during recent safety briefings and toolbox talks. The answers are provided for clarification.

4.1 Q: Can I make a small adjustment to the grinder while it is still winding down, just to save time?

A: No. Section 2.2 of this briefing is clear: no adjustment is permitted while the wheel is spinning, regardless of how long the machine takes to stop. Wait until the wheel has come to a complete stop and the machine is isolated. This is not negotiable.

Track Maintenance Survey Q3 2024 – Responses

Survey Summary
Period: 1 October 2024 – 31 October 2024
Administered by: PCRMD Safety Team
Purpose: Collect worker feedback on safety, workload, and equipment
Status: Historical record – survey closed, results compiled for management review

Response Rate
The Q3 Survey summary notes a response rate of 72 percent. Record status: historical. This is recorded as the final historical figure for the quarter, based on completed returns received by the close of the survey window. A total of 214 survey forms were distributed across the three depots, and 154 valid responses were received. The remaining 60 forms were either not returned or were received after the cutoff date and therefore excluded from the analysis.

Anonymised responses are presented below, grouped by theme. Comments are reproduced as written, including minor typographical errors, to preserve the original voice of respondents. No names or crew identifiers have been retained.

Safety

Summary of Safety Ratings (Q3 2024)

Open-ended comments on safety:

- "The new hi-vis vests are good but they make you sweat a lot in the afternoon heat. Can we get a lighter material for summer?"
- "Safety briefings are fine but sometimes they run too long and we lose track. Keep it short and to the point."
- "We need more night shifts. The day work on the mainline is dangerous with all the traffic passing at speed."
- "The rail temp was 48C last week, ballast dusty, and we still had to keep going. That felt unsafe. We should stop work when it gets that hot."
- "First aid kits on the trolleys are well stocked now, good improvement from last quarter."
- "Someone left a crowbar on the track near the crossover on the 14th. Lucky it was spotted before a train came. Please remind everyone to do a final walk down."
- "The new warning lights at the level crossing are much better. Can we get them at the other crossing too?"

Workload

- "More rostered days off would help. We get told to take breaks but then the work doesnt get done and it falls on the next shift."
- "Paperwork is taking too long. We spend an hour at the end of each shift filling in forms that could be done on a tablet in the field."
- "The workload is fair most weeks, but when a train is delayed the whole plan shifts and we have to rush."
- "Can we have a second person on the ballast tamper? Its a two man job and weve been doing it solo since the roster change."

Equipment

2.3 The following hazard classes are present in our workplace and require specific attention:
- Diesel and fuel oils – flammable, skin irritant

2.4 When transferring substances between containers, label the new container immediately with the product name and hazard pictograms.

3. EMERGENCY PROCEDURES

3.1 Emergency assembly points are marked at each worksite. Know the assembly point for your location before commencing work.

3.2 In the event of an emergency:
- Stop work immediately
- Warn others in your vicinity
- Follow the directions of the emergency coordinator or authorised person
- Do not re-enter the area until advised it is safe

3.3 Fire extinguishers are located at all worksites and in buildings. Know the location of the nearest extinguisher. Only use an extinguisher if you have been trained and the fire is small enough to be safely controlled.

3.4 First aid kits are available at each worksite and in the depot office. Report all injuries, however minor, to your supervisor and record them in the injury register.

3.5 If you discover a fire, activate the alarm and call the emergency number. Give your location clearly and do not hang up until the operator confirms they have the information.

4. TRACK CLEARANCE REQUIREMENTS

4.1 The Authority's directive mandates minimum track clearance of 600 mm. Record status: current. This clearance applies to all personnel, tools, and equipment when working on or near the track.

4.2 The 600 mm clearance is measured from the nearest running rail face to the closest point of the person, tool, or equipment. This distance is the minimum separation required at all times, including during work activities, rest periods, and when moving along the track.

4.3 The clearance requirement applies to:
- Personnel walking along or across the track
- Hand tools, including hammers, bars, and measuring equipment
- Plant and machinery, including trolleys, grinders, and tampers
- Materials stored temporarily at the worksite
- Personal items such as bags, lunchboxes, and water bottles

4.4 Where it is not possible to maintain 600 mm clearance due to the nature of the work, a safe system of work must be implemented. This may include:
- Possession of the track (absolute occupation)
- Track occupancy authority with appropriate protection
- Lookout working, where approved for the specific location and conditions

4.5 The 600 mm clearance is a minimum. Greater clearance must be provided where:
- Trains are travelling at high speed
- The track is curved and sight distance is limited
- Weather conditions reduce visibility
- The worksite is in a tunnel or cutting
- Plant or equipment is being operated

4.6 Do not place tools or materials closer than 600 mm to the running rail, even temporarily. If you need to put something down while working, place it on the opposite side of the track or at a safe distance.

4.7 Check that your worksite layout maintains the clearance before work commences and after any change in activities. The person in charge of the worksite is responsible for ensuring compliance.

4.8 If you observe any situation where the 600 mm clearance cannot be maintained, stop work and report to your supervisor immediately. Do not attempt to continue working in a non-compliant position.

5. TRACKSIDE SAFETY

5.1 Always be aware of train movements. Trains can approach without warning and may be quieter than expected, especially in wet conditions or when carrying certain loads.

5.2 When walking along the track:
- Walk in the direction facing approaching traffic where possible
- Keep as far from the running rail as practicable
- Do not walk on the rail head or in the four-foot
- Cross the track only at designated crossing points or where you have a clear view in both directions

SAFETY BRIEFING 2024-11
ISSUED: 4 November 2024
EFFECTIVE: Immediately
ISSUING OFFICE: PCRMD Safety Office
DISTRIBUTION: All staff, contractors, and visitors

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 This briefing supplements the PCRMD Safety Management System and the Track Work Safety Manual. It applies to all rail maintenance activities, including planned works, fault response, inspections, and possessions.

1.2 This briefing remains in effect until superseded. A record of this briefing is held in the safety office. Safety Briefing 2024-11 issued date 2024-11-04 date. Record status: historical.

1.3 All supervisors must confirm that their teams have read and understood this briefing before commencing work. Confirmation is to be recorded on the team briefing sheet and returned to the safety office by close of business Friday 8 November 2024.

2. HAZARD ALERTS – RECENT INCIDENTS

2.1 Incident: Near miss with track vehicle at the Westport yard crossover, 28 October 2024.

A track vehicle moved through the crossover while a small team was walking back to the compound after completing a ballast inspection. The lookout was in position but was focused on the main line rather than the yard lead. The vehicle operator sounded the horn and the team cleared the track with approximately 20 seconds to spare.

Contributing factors:
- Lookout positioned on the wrong side of the group
- Yard movements not included in the pre-work risk assessment
- Team walked along the track instead of the designated walkway

Actions required:
- Yard and depot movements must be included in the pre-work brief even when the work is on the main line
- Lookouts must position themselves to cover all possible approach directions
- Use the designated walkway whenever it is available, even if it adds time

2.2 Incident: Hand injury during rail grinding, 30 October 2024.

A crew member sustained a crush injury to the left hand while adjusting a grinding stone. The machine was not isolated and the crew member placed their hand between the stone and the guard while the wheel was still spinning down.

Contributing factors:
- Machine not isolated before adjustment
- Crew member attempting a quick adjustment rather than stopping the machine
- Inadequate supervision of the task

Actions required:
- All adjustments to grinding equipment must be carried out with the machine isolated and the wheel at a complete stop
- No adjustment is permitted while the wheel is spinning, regardless of how long the machine takes to stop
- Supervisors must check that isolation is in place before any adjustment begins

2.3 Incident: Spotting of a broken rail near the 87.4 km mark, 1 November 2024.

A track patrol identified a broken rail on the down line. The rail had a transverse break at the web. The patrol reported it immediately and the line was blocked. No train passed over the break.

Actions required:
- Continue to report any suspected rail defect immediately, even if you are not certain
- Do not attempt to assess the severity of a defect while trains are running
- Ensure your patrol route includes checking the full rail section, not just the head

2.4 Hazard alert: Increased kangaroo activity on the corridor between the 92 km and 98 km marks.

Recent reports indicate a higher than usual number of kangaroos moving across the track in this section, particularly around dawn and dusk. While this is not a direct track worker hazard, it can cause distractions and sudden movements by drivers of track vehicles.

Actions required:
- Reduce speed when driving track vehicles through this section at dawn and dusk
- Be alert for animals moving onto the track ahead of you
- Report any collisions or near misses with animals to your supervisor

2.5 Hazard alert: Dusty ballast conditions in the cuttings near the 74 km mark.

The recent dry weather has left ballast dusty in the cuttings. This reduces visibility when working near the track and can make footing unstable on slopes.

Actions required:
- Use additional caution when walking or working on ballast in these areas
- Wear dust masks if dust is affecting your breathing
- Water down the area if dust becomes excessive and this is practical

Safety Briefing 2024-11
Briefing No. 2024-11-04
Issue Date: 4 November 2024
Effective: Immediately

This briefing is issued to all track maintenance, patrol, and track vehicle staff. It follows the incident and hazard alerts in the earlier sections of this briefing (Sections 2.1 to 2.5). Please read this entire document carefully, sign the acknowledgement sheet at the end, and return it to your supervisor by 8 November 2024.

Section 3 – General Safety Reminders

The following reminders apply to all work activities on the corridor, regardless of the specific task. They are not new rules, but they are frequently overlooked. Please treat them as mandatory.

3.1 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

- Hard hat, hi-vis vest, and safety boots are to be worn at all times when on or near the track. This includes walking to and from the work site, and during breaks if you are still within the track corridor.
- Safety glasses should be worn when grinding, cutting, or doing any task that may produce flying particles. If you wear prescription glasses, you must wear approved over-glasses.
- Hearing protection must be worn when operating or working near powered equipment, including grinders, tampers, and generators. If you have to raise your voice to be heard by someone an arm's length away, you need hearing protection.
- Gloves are required for handling rail, sleepers, ballast, or any material with sharp edges. Do not wear gloves when operating rotating machinery such as grinders or drills – they can get caught.
- Dust masks are to be worn where dust is present, including the dusty ballast conditions mentioned in Section 2.5. If you are unsure whether a mask is needed, ask your supervisor.

3.2 Track Access and Lookout

- Never enter the track corridor without a valid track access permit and a current briefing on the day's protection arrangements.
- If you are working under a lookout, you must maintain voice or radio contact with the lookout at all times. If you lose contact, stop work and move to a safe location.
- The lookout's instructions are to be followed immediately, without question. Do not stop to gather tools or equipment – your safety is more important than any tool.
- When walking along the track, always face oncoming traffic unless you are specifically instructed otherwise. Stay clear of the gauge corner of the rail where possible.
- Do not cross the track at unprotected locations. Use the designated crossing points.

3.3 Track Vehicle Operation

- All track vehicles must be operated by a person holding the appropriate competency for that vehicle type.
- Conduct a pre-start inspection of the vehicle each day before use. Check brakes, lights, horns, and any attachments.
- Do not carry passengers unless the vehicle is fitted with approved seating and seatbelts for the number of passengers.
- When driving through the corridor, particularly in the sections with increased kangaroo activity (92 km to 98 km), reduce speed and be prepared to stop suddenly.
- Never leave a track vehicle unattended on the line unless it has been properly secured and the area protected.

3.4 Manual Handling and Lifting

- Assess the load before lifting. If it is too heavy or awkward, use a mechanical aid or get help.
- Use proper lifting technique: bend at the knees, keep your back straight, and hold the load close to your body.
- Do not twist your body while carrying a load. Turn your feet first.
- Report any manual handling injuries, no matter how minor, to your supervisor.

Section 4 – Frequently Asked Questions

The following questions have been raised by staff during recent safety briefings and toolbox talks. The answers are provided for clarification.

4.1 Q: Can I make a small adjustment to the grinder while it is still winding down, just to save time?

A: No. Section 2.2 of this briefing is clear: no adjustment is permitted while the wheel is spinning, regardless of how long the machine takes to stop. Wait until the wheel has come to a complete stop and the machine is isolated. This is not negotiable.
